core.text: To say whose something is, Latin puts the owner into **the genitive (the 'of' form)**, *genitīvus possessīvus*: *fīlius Iūliī* = the son of Julius, Julius's son; *ancilla Aemiliae* = Aemilia's maid. Owner and thing owned need not stand side by side; the ending shows the link. The question word is *cuius?* (whose?).
English shows possession with *'s* or *of*: *the man's house*, *the roof of the house*. Latin uses one ending for both and no *of*.
The owner takes the genitive: singular -ae (a-nouns), -ī (us- and um-nouns); plural -ārum, -ōrum. It may stand before or after the noun it belongs to.

invented.en: The master's stick is in the garden.

core.text: *Puellae* is the genitive (of the girl) and also the dative (the 'to/for' form), to the girl; *servī* is genitive singular (of the slave) and nominative plural (slaves). Look at the neighbours: a genitive hangs on another noun (*liber puellae* — the girl's book); a dative hangs on a verb of giving (*puellae librum dat* — gives the girl a book).

more.text: From the learner's notes: grammatical 'possession' is broad. It covers holding something (the student's library book), owning it (my book on your shelf), and simply a close tie (the man's wife). English pronouns still have a genitive (*his*, *her*, *whose*), and English always puts the possessor first; Latin may put it either side of its noun and even split the two with another word (*pānēs sunt fēminae*).

Ørberg cap. II: genetīvus -ī / -ōrum for masculine and neuter, -ae / -ārum for feminine, with the question *cuius?*. Names in -ius have genitive -iī (*Iūliī*), often written with one ī. For 'my', 'your', 'his own' Latin does not use a genitive but the adjectives *meus*, *tuus*, *suus*, which agree with the thing owned: *servus meus*, *ancilla tua*. For 'his' meaning someone else's it uses *eius*. A&G §343.
